description: Hello from Team Apache! We are tackling the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our mission is to design an interactive training module that brings the reality of spaceflight to kids. We are actively looking for new members with interests in Coding, Web Development or Astrophysics to help bring our vision to life. If you are ready to innovate, join us!
summary:
Project Apache is an interactive STEM mission simulator designed to teach students ages 10–16 the real systems-engineering trade-offs of living on Mars. Space games often oversimplify survival mechanics or overwhelm learners with graduate-level math. Project Apache places cadets in command of a four-astronaut outpost at Jezero Crater for ten Martian Sols, challenging them to balance finite power from a Kilopower fission core and dust-attenuated solar arrays across four coupled subsystems: life support (O₂/CO₂ scrubbing), cabin heating, hydroponic food production, and active radiation shielding.

Powered by real NASA DONKI space-weather flare alerts, NASA InSight Martian weather telemetry, and official NASA life-support baselines, every decision triggers realistic physical consequences. When an X-class solar storm hits, diverting kilowatts to shielding forces tough choices between crop growth, warmth, and battery reserves. An interactive Habitat Digital Twin and plain-English Flight Director debriefs transform abstract habitat physics into a memorable, classroom-ready engineering experience.
details: Project Apache is a web-based Martian outpost simulator where students command a four-astronaut habitat at Jezero Crater over ten Martian Sols. Powered by live telemetry from NASA’s DONKI space-weather API, InSight Mars weather data, and NASA life-support engineering baselines, the app challenges cadets to manage a coupled power grid and closed-loop habitat. Each Sol, players allocate kilowatts from a steady 40 kW Kilopower fission reactor, battery bank, and dust-attenuated solar arrays across four interconnected subsystems: oxygen/CO₂ life support, cabin heating, hydroponic farming, and active radiation shielding. Overdrawing power triggers realistic brownouts, while cold temperatures slow crop photosynthesis and CO₂ scrubbing. When NASA flare alerts inject high-energy solar radiation or dust storms darken the sky, students must rebalance energy in real time. An interactive SVG Habitat Digital Twin, vital telemetry graphs, and plain-English Flight Director debriefs reveal the immediate physical consequences of every engineering decision.
